1:
Cyril identifies the men. They were followers of the opinions of Judas of Galilee, whom Luke mentions in the Acts, holding that no man ought to be called master; great numbers of them refused to acknowledge Caesar and were punished for it, and they held besides that no sacrifice might be offered which the law of Moses had not ordained, so forbidding the offerings made for the safety of the Emperor and the Roman people. Pilate, enraged, had them killed in the midst of the very victims they thought themselves entitled to offer, so that the blood of the offerers ran with the blood of the offerings. Wesley gives the same identification in a sentence and adds that they were surrounded and slain while worshipping in the temple at a public feast. Robertson supposes rather an insurrection against the Roman government whose leaders were cut down in the temple courts while the sacrifices were going on.

No other historian records it, as Ellicott and Robertson both observe, and both reckon it entirely in character for the governor whose other outrages are on record. Ellicott guesses at an outburst of zealous fanaticism among pilgrims from that province, repressed with the ruthlessness shown in his other tumults, and thinks it probably one cause of the enmity between Herod and Pilate noticed later in the Gospel. Henry knows Josephus’s account of Samaritans killed on their way to Gerizim and refuses to identify the two stories, suggesting instead that these men, being Herod’s subjects, may only have been suspected of belonging to the faction and murdered because its real partisans were out of reach. Lightfoot leaves the date open: if the news came immediately after the deed, the massacre fell shortly before the feast of Dedication, since the journey towards that feast begins a few verses on; but whether the tellers brought it as news not yet heard or only to draw out an opinion is itself undecided. He also doubts the identification with Judas’s sect, on the ground that Christ would hardly have offered any kind of defence for such men.

Why the story was told is the question each of them presses. The Gloss notices the sequence, that after speaking of the punishments of sinners he is fitly told of the punishment of particular sinners, and takes occasion from it to denounce vengeance against others. Cyril thinks the tellers had a purpose: it was generally believed that these Galileans had been most justly punished as sowers of offence among the people, and the rulers relate the matter to excite the people’s hatred against him while discovering what he thought. Barnes canvasses the possibilities — a wish to get an opinion on the governor’s conduct and so involve the speaker with the reigning powers of Judea, or the mere passing on of news — and infers from the reply that they supposed the men had deserved what they got.

Ambrose and Bede read the horror as a figure. Ambrose finds in it a mystical type touching all who, under the Devil’s compulsion, offer an impure sacrifice and whose prayer is itself a sin, as was written of Judas, who devised the betrayal of his Lord’s blood while he was among the sacrifices. Bede works from the name, which he interprets as the mouth of the hammerer and takes for the devil ever ready to strike: blood stands for sin and the sacrifices for good actions, so that the mingling happens whenever the devil stains the alms and other good works of the faithful, whether by carnal indulgence or by courting the praise of men.
2:
Barnes reads the question as exposing an assumption. From the answer it appears that the tellers supposed the manner of the death proved the men to have been very great sinners, and they are told that the conclusion is not a right one — a sudden and violent end is no proof that those who meet it are peculiarly wicked. Ellicott puts the same point as a correction of a whole habit of interpretation: the tale had been told with a conviction, expressed or implied, that the massacre was a special judgment on special and exceptional guilt, and the reply sweeps away such rash constructions of the divine government at a stroke. Robertson parses the comparison itself, the preposition meaning beside and so beyond, these men set alongside all the other Galileans; and he notes that the perfect tense marks what they suffered as an irrevocable fact. Gill observes what the answer carefully does not do: it neither approves nor condemns the governor’s action, and though it allows the men to have been sinners it does not bear hard on them, but turns the instance to the conviction of the hearers.

Calvin finds two faults in the attitude being corrected, and thinks the passage useful for that alone. The disease is almost natural to us, he says, to be rigorous and severe in judging others and too ready to flatter our own faults, so that we not only censure our brethren’s offences with excessive severity but condemn them as wicked and reprobate the moment any calamity overtakes them; while every man who is not sorely pressed by the hand of God slumbers at ease in the midst of his sins, as though God were favourable and reconciled to him. Both halves are errors. When God chastises someone before our eyes he is warning us of his judgments, so that each may examine himself and consider what he deserves; and when he spares us for a time, that forbearance is so far from being an occasion for slumber that it ought to be read the other way.

Barnes adds a note on the method rather than the doctrine. The occasion was used contrary to what the tellers expected, and turned from their question about other men’s guilt into a warning about their own danger; and he observes that no suitable occasion was ever let pass without some such warning to the wicked and some entreaty to forsake their ways, the subject being always present to that mind and introduced easily and fully.
3:
Gill states the denial plainly: they were not greater sinners than their neighbours, and nothing of the kind follows from the bloody slaughter made of them, since others who escaped such an end might deserve it far more. Robertson reads the condition grammatically and finds the repentance continuous — a present subjunctive, a changing of mind and conduct kept up rather than done once — in a condition left undetermined but with the prospect of being determined, while the verb for perishing stands in the middle voice and is intransitive.

How far the word likewise reaches divides two of them. Wesley takes it strictly, as the Greek implies: all those of Galilee and of Jerusalem should perish in the very same manner, and so they did, there being a remarkable resemblance between the fate of these men and that of the main body of the nation, whose flower was slain at Jerusalem by the Roman sword while assembled at one of the great festivals, with many thousands perishing in the temple itself and literally buried under its ruins. Ellicott will not have it pressed so far: some of those who heard may have fallen by the sword of Titus as these had fallen by the sword of Pilate, but hardly all the impenitent, and the manner of death named in the next verse could not be said of them at all.

Chrysostom sets the warning against the two ways God is said to deal with sinners. Some he punishes here, cutting off their iniquities and appointing them a lighter reckoning hereafter, or perhaps releasing them entirely, and correcting by their punishment others who are living in wickedness. Others he does not punish at all, so that if they take heed to themselves by repentance they escape both the present penalty and the future, but if they continue in their sins they suffer still greater torment. Titus of Bostra adds the governing principle, that whatever judgments are passed for the punishment of the guilty happen not only by the authority of the judges but by the will of God, so that whether a judge acts on strict grounds of conscience or has some other object in his sentence, the work is to be ascribed to divine appointment.
4:
Barnes traces the name through the Bible and out of it. As applied to water it occurs only three times in the Scriptures — once as running water in Isaiah, once as a pool near the king’s garden in Nehemiah, and once as the pool in the healing of the man born blind — while Josephus mentions the fountain frequently, placing it where the Valley of the Cheese-mongers opens out, on the south side of Mount Moriah and between it and the Valley of Jehoshaphat, the water in his own day flowing from a small artificial basin under the cliff. Robertson says few sites have been more clearly located. Lightfoot nevertheless leaves one thing open: whether the tower stood over the pool’s porches or somewhat away from it in the quarter that still carried the name, since the pool itself bears that name and he doubts whether grammar allows the article to be prefixed to a district. He inclines to a tower over the porticoes, which would have overwhelmed the men while they were busy purifying themselves or waiting for the water to be troubled — a circumstance that makes the parallel with the Galileans closer than it first looks. Clarke makes the same conjecture in a line.

Ellicott suspects the governor stands behind this disaster as well as the other. The incident is again recorded nowhere else, and it had clearly impressed men with horror as a special judgment. Since the pool belonged to the water system of the city, he thinks it not unlikely that the tower formed part of the aqueduct works Pilate had planned and partly executed, and for which he appropriated some of the sacred treasure of the Temple; and if that is right, the popular anger that measure provoked would make the fall of the structure look to many like a divine verdict on the whole undertaking.

Clarke and Robertson both notice that the word has changed. These are not called sinners, as the Galileans were, but debtors — a Jewish way of speaking of sinners which Robertson insists on rendering literally against the Authorized Version. Clarke draws out the force of the change: men professing to stand under the law are bound by it to obey every precept, and those who do not are reckoned debtors to the law, or rather to the divine justice from which the law came, so that the question falls on people living in Jerusalem who thought themselves peculiarly attached to it. Barnes observes that this second case is volunteered rather than reported, probably a recent one and probably judged by the hearers exactly as they had judged the first; and Robertson makes the method itself the point, public events used twice over to teach a spiritual lesson, with a moral drawn from the massacre and a moral drawn from the accident.
5:
Gill affirms the denial and keeps the providence: they were not greater sinners than others, though so melancholy a thing befell them, and it did not befall them outside the providence of God. Barnes states the principle at large. It is improper to suppose that those on whom heavy judgments fall in this world are the worst of men, because this is not a world of retribution: often the most wicked are suffered to prosper and their punishment is reserved for another world, while the righteous are called to suffer much and appear to lie under the sore displeasure of God, as the psalmist complains. What may be known is that the wicked will not always escape, that God is just, and that nobody who suffers here or hereafter suffers more than he deserves; what seems unequal now will be made equal and plain in the world to come.

Robertson marks a difference of tense between this warning and the one two verses earlier. There the subjunctive was present and the repentance continuous; here it is aorist, and the demand is for an immediate turning, though he notes that the editors put the other form in the margin. He concedes that the interpretation of accidents is a difficult matter, and holds that the moral pointed out is in any case obvious.

Clarke takes the word for likewise strictly — in a like way, in the same manner — and holds that the prediction was literally fulfilled: when the city fell to the Romans, multitudes of the priests were cut down as they went on with their offerings, so that their own blood ran among the blood of the victims, while multitudes more were buried beneath the fallen walls and temple, as Josephus records at length. Yet Clarke will not let the fulfilment be used to rank the sufferers. It is very wrong, he says, to suppose that those who fall by the sword or by natural accident are the most culpable before God, since no adequate punishment for sin can be inflicted in this world at all; what God does in this way he does in general, to alarm others by mercy, to show his hatred of sin, to keep in men’s minds a proper sense of his providence and justice, and to give sinners in one or two particular instances a general intimation of what they deserve.
6:
Titus of Bostra supplies the provocation: the Jews were boasting that while the eighteen had perished they themselves all remained unhurt, and the parable is set before them on that account. Henry ties it to the warning just uttered, that except they be reformed they will be ruined, as a barren tree that bears no fruit will be cut down. Gill takes it as spoken at the same time and on the same occasion, setting out God’s patience towards the nation, its unfruitfulness, and the danger of destruction failing amendment. Ellicott hears behind it the Baptist’s sharper saying, that every tree which brings forth no good fruit is hewn down, here expanded into a story; and he notes that the joint culture of fig tree and vine was common enough to have passed into a proverb.

Ambrose thinks the choice of tree exact. It abounds in wide and spreading foliage and deceives its owner with the vain expectation of promised fruit, as in the synagogue the teachers are unfruitful in good works yet magnify themselves with words as with abundant leaves, the empty shadow of the law stretching far and wide. He adds a grower’s observation, that this is the only tree which puts out fruit in the place of flowers, and that its fruit falls so that other fruit may succeed it, though some few of the first remain and do not fall. Bede keeps the same identification and makes the visit historical: the Lord who had established the synagogue by Moses came born in the flesh, taught in the synagogue often, sought there the fruits of faith, and in the hearts of the Pharisees found none.

Others take the tree more widely. Augustine makes it the race of mankind, since the first man after sinning covered his nakedness with fig leaves; Theophylact makes it each of us, planted in the vineyard of God, that is in the Church or in the world, and takes the interceding husbandman for any holy man who prays within the Church for those outside it. Clarke works out a key point by point, with God as the owner, the Jewish Church as the tree, Judea as the vineyard, the fruit sought as righteousness proportioned to the culture bestowed, the dresser as Christ to whom all judgment is committed, and the felling as the unsheathing of the Roman sword. Wesley allows two distributions of the parts, the Father as owner with Christ as keeper, or Christ as owner with his ministers as keepers. Ambrose knows the wider reading too, and judges that those who take the tree for wickedness rather than for the synagogue differ in nothing from what has gone before except in choosing the genus instead of the species.

On the seeking itself Ambrose denies any ignorance in it: the owner sought not because he did not know the tree was barren, but to show in a figure that the synagogue ought by that time to have had fruit. He marks a threefold coming — to Abraham, to Moses, to Mary, which is to say in the seal of the covenant, in the law, and in the body — with purification, sanctification and justification answering to the three, and finds the people incapable of the first because theirs was the circumcision of the body and not of the heart. Gregory widens the three years to the whole history: man’s nature was sought before the law, under the law, and under grace, by waiting, admonishing and visiting, and the complaint of finding nothing holds against men whose hearts are neither corrected by the law of nature breathed into them, nor instructed by precepts, nor converted by the miracles of the incarnation.
7:
Whether the three years are a date divides them sharply. Barnes refuses to make them one: the words are not to be referred to the length of Christ’s preaching as though an exact term were specified, but mean, within the story, that the owner had long looked for fruit and been disappointed three years running — long enough to prove the tree barren. Robertson agrees and adds a grower’s correction, that the three years run from the time the tree would normally be expected to bear and not from its planting; he takes the nation to be meant, and notes that the later withering of a barren fig tree at Jerusalem turns the parable into an object lesson. Clarke builds the opposite case into a chronology: the circumstance implies that the ministry had already run three years, and the year of reprieve asked for puts the parable about twelve months before the crucifixion, making the whole public ministry about four years — from which he infers that the parable does not belong where it appears to be placed, this evangelist never studying chronological arrangement. Wesley splits the difference, holding that Christ was then in the third year of his ministry while allowing that a certain number may stand for an uncertain one.

The word for cumbering gets more weight than it looks able to bear. Barnes says it means to render the ground sterile: by drawing up the juices of the earth the useless tree impoverished the soil and hindered the neighbouring vines, so that it was not merely good for nothing but actively doing mischief. Ellicott presses the Greek further still, that it implies positive injury rather than mere encumbrance and is commonly rendered by bringing to nought, and he produces a line of Shakespeare’s to show that the English verb once carried the same force. Wesley puts it in a sentence, that the tree bore no fruit itself and took up the ground of another that would. Clarke supplies the owner’s reasoning, that it should come down so a more profitable tree might be planted in its place.

Lightfoot brings in the law that stood against felling. No tree of a fruit-bearing kind might be cut down lightly or on any small occasion, Deuteronomy providing against it, and the rabbinic commentary observes that both an affirmative and a negative command are given there, so that felling such a tree is doubly forbidden except on a thoroughly indispensable occasion. He quotes the sayings that grew up around the rule — not to cut down a palm that still bears a cab of dates, nor an olive that bears so much as a quarter of one — and the remark of one rabbi that his son would not have died had he not cut down a fig tree before its time. Gill distributes the parts of the parable differently from the rest: if the owner is the Father the dresser must be Christ, but since the owner seems rather to be Christ himself, the dressers may be the ministers of the word, to whom he lets out his vineyard to cultivate and to keep its fruit.
8:
Gill offers two accounts of who is speaking, and prefers the second. If the owner is the Father, the petition may stand for Christ’s intercession with him — not only for the elect, the unconverted that they may be converted and the converted for sanctification, for fresh discoveries of pardon, for consolation under trouble and for final perseverance, but also for his enemies, for profane sinners and formal professors, for the sake of his own people among them, so that divine judgments are held off at least for a time; and the nation was in fact spared a while after this, though by then deserving immediate destruction. Gill thinks it likelier, though, that the intercession of Christ’s ministers and other good men is meant, who do for a sinful nation and a barren church what Abraham did for Sodom and Moses and Aaron for Israel.

The threat itself is read as an act of mercy. It belongs to God’s mercy, says Basil, not to inflict punishment silently but to send out threatenings which recall the sinner to repentance, as happened with the men of Nineveh; on that reading the sentence of felling is spoken in order to rouse the dresser to care for the tree and to stir the barren soil to bring forth its proper fruit. Gregory Nazianzen turns it into a rule for those who must correct others: let us not strike suddenly but overcome by gentleness, lest we cut down a fig tree still able to bear, which the care of a skilful dresser might yet restore.

On the husbandry the commentators go literal and figurative by turns. Lightfoot reports the practice from the rabbis: dung is laid in the gardens to moisten the earth, the roots are dug about, suckers plucked up, leaves taken off, ashes sprinkled, and smoke made under the trees to kill the worms. Robertson keeps to the plain sense — cast dung around it, manure it — noting that the word stands nowhere else in the New Testament. Ellicott makes the homeliness the point, since the image suggests fertilising and gracious influences no less vividly than dew or rain from heaven, and points perhaps to those which work on us through our earthly surroundings rather than to the directly supernatural action of grace. Augustine and Theophylact allegorise both operations: to dig about the tree is to teach humility and patience, ground that has been dug being lowly ground, while the dung stands for soiled garments, which is to say the grief and mourning of sinners, since those who do penance truly are in soiled garments.
9:
Robertson names the figure in the sentence: it breaks off suddenly for effect, as elsewhere in Mark and in Acts, leaving the reader to supply what should follow. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the manuscripts, some of the better copies reading that it bear fruit in the time to come, and on either reading the sentence is elliptical, so that English has to insert a word to carry the sense. Gill fills out the happy half of it: if barren professors become fruitful it is well for themselves, since they shall eat the fruit of their doings; well for the churches where they are, since good works are profitable to men; and well for the owner and the dresser both, since when Christ has his fruit from his churches his ministers have theirs. Robertson adds a traveller’s footnote, that Trench reports a story of this very kind still current among the Arabs, an intercession for a fig tree for one year more on the promise that this time it will certainly bear.

Calvin states the substance of the whole parable at this point, and it is not encouraging. Many are endured for a time who deserve to be cut off, but they gain nothing by the delay if they persist in their obstinacy. The flattery that hardens hypocrites and makes them more obstinate comes from this, that they never think of their sins until they are compelled to; so long as God winks at them and puts off his chastisements they imagine he is well satisfied with them, and indulge themselves the more freely for it, which is why Paul speaks so earnestly of men treasuring up the wrath of God against the last day.

The husbandry Calvin reads the same way. It is well known, he says, that trees are sometimes kept not because their owners find them useful and productive, but because a careful and industrious husbandman makes every possible trial and experiment on them before he determines to take them out; so the year granted is an experiment and not a reprieve, and the sentence already passed is suspended rather than cancelled. On that account the unfinished clause carries its own warning: the alternative is stated plainly enough in the next breath, and the silence falls only on the better half.
10:
Ambrose ties the scene back to the parable just told: the speaker soon made clear that he had been talking about the synagogue, and showed that he truly came to it by preaching in it. Chrysostom describes the manner of the teaching — not apart but in the synagogues, calmly, wavering in nothing and determining nothing against the law of Moses, and on the Sabbath because that was when the Jews were engaged in hearing the law. Robertson notes only the periphrastic imperfect; Henry makes more of it, reading the construction as a continued act, so that he still taught the people knowledge and was in his element while teaching, and drawing the rule that religious assemblies are a divine institution to be attended though they number but two or three, since nobody spends a Sabbath as well at home with a good book.

Where the story came from interests Ellicott and Calvin. Ellicott observes that what follows is peculiar to this Gospel, and that the indefiniteness about time and place suggests one of the previously unrecorded traditions the writer met with when he began his own search for materials — a guess he thinks partly confirmed by the title used of Christ a few verses later. Calvin says outright that he has set some events reported only by this Evangelist in immediate connection without reference to dates, the writers not having cared much for exactness on that point. Gill locates the synagogue loosely in Galilee or Judea and supplies the local colour, that larger cities had more than one, Jerusalem being credited with three hundred and ninety-four on one reckoning and as many as four hundred and eighty by other writers.

Chrysostom lays down here the principle that will be turned against the ruler of the synagogue shortly. God rested from the works of the world and not from holy works, since his own working is constant and everlasting, as the Son says that his Father works until now and he works; so that what should cease in us after the likeness of God is our worldly business and not our religious.

Gregory reads the woman as the fig tree in figure. Human nature rushes of its own will into sin and, refusing to bear the fruit of obedience, loses the state of uprightness, so that the bowed woman is the barren tree and the woman made upright is the tree preserved. Ambrose keeps the tree for the synagogue and makes the infirm woman a figure of the Church instead, which, having fulfilled the measure of the law and of the resurrection and been raised on high into the eternal resting place, can no longer feel the frailty of our weak inclinations. He then counts: ten sentences contain the perfection of the law and the number eight the fullness of the resurrection, so that this woman could not be healed unless she had fulfilled law and grace together.
11:
Ellicott credits the description to a trained observer. The duration of the affliction, the symptoms of a permanent curvature of the spine, and the very form of the two participles — bent together, unable to unbend — are all characteristic of such a writer. Robertson agrees and names the terms, the first a medical word for curvature of the spine, found nowhere else in the New Testament, and the second its negative counterpart, so that she could not straighten herself at all and had to come in bent double. Barnes takes the eighteen years as evidence that the miracle was real and the disease not feigned. Wesley, remarking that to many it must have looked like a natural distemper, asks whether a modern physician would not have called it a nervous case.

What the phrase about a spirit means is handled more cautiously. Robertson construes it as a spirit which caused the weakness, a genitive of the same kind as the spirit of bondage. Cyril takes it that she suffered from the cruelty of the devil, left to him on account of her own faults or through the transgression of Adam, by which men’s bodies incur infirmity and death; and he holds that God grants the devil such power precisely so that men, pressed down by the weight of their adversity, may betake themselves to better things. Calvin argues from the silence about symptoms that the disease was not of an ordinary kind nor one physicians understood, which is why it is named as it is: unusual and extraordinary diseases are for the most part inflicted through the agency of the devil, and that made the display of divine power triumphing over Satan the more striking — though Calvin is careful to add that Satan does not rule men at his pleasure. Clarke arranges the whole episode under three heads and traces the origin to sin, since had sin never entered the world there would have been neither pain nor distortion nor death, and the agency to Satan, adding his suspicion that the chief part of unaccountable and inexplicable disorders still comes from the same quarter. Lightfoot reports that the Jews distinguished spirits from devils and from ministering angels, and admits he cannot say in what sense they took the middle term.

That she was in the synagogue at all is pressed by three of them. Gill makes it a rebuke: infirm as she is described, she got out to the place of worship, which may shame those who on every trifling indisposition keep at home and excuse themselves from attending the house of God. Barnes says the same more gently, that the sanctuary is where the afflicted find consolation and that it was there the Saviour met her. Ellicott infers habitual devotion from her presence, and with it the faith which made her receptive of the healing power. Basil supplies the figure that gives her posture its meaning, that it is the head of the brutes which is bent towards the ground and looks upon it.
12:
Barnes calls the declaration remarkable, and the reason is what precedes it: there is no sign that she asked for anything. She was addressed, and the disease departed; and Barnes reckons the proofs of Messiahship clear in such a case, and the power mighty which could restore her by a word. Robertson notes that she was called over to him first, and that the perfect passive means loosed so as to stay loosed, this being the only place in the New Testament where that common verb is used of a disease. Gill fixes the moment in the synagogue among the people, either during the teaching or just after it. Henry sets the cure beside the discourse it interrupted, as a miracle wrought to confirm the doctrine preached and recommend it as worthy of acceptance — and a miracle of mercy at that.

Ellicott makes the tense carry the point. He would render it that she has been loosed, the verb standing in the perfect, so that the work of healing was complete before she moved; and on that reading the words are a test of her faith, the question being whether on hearing them she would attempt what she had not done for eighteen years.

Calvin finds power and grace exhibited together. The miracle testifies that he had come for the purpose of relieving the wretched, which is the grace of it; and the power appears in the wording, since he authoritatively declares that the deliverance stood at his own disposal, while employing at the same time the outward sign whose use Calvin has explained elsewhere. The two cannot be separated in the sentence: the woman is told what has happened to her rather than promised what may, and the telling is itself the act.

Cyril treats the cure as evidence of what the Incarnation was for. That the Word was manifested to destroy corruption and death, and the devil’s hatred against us, he holds to be plain from the actual events rather than from argument; and a bondage inflicted through that hatred, undone here in a single sentence, is one of the events he means. On that reading the loosing is not simply a kindness done to one sufferer but a specimen of the whole undertaking, which is why the word used of it is the word for releasing a prisoner.
13:
Gill notes that the hands were laid on her as the words were spoken, which was sometimes the way of it in these cures. Robertson describes the gesture as that of the Great Physician with gentle kindness, and takes the verb for the straightening in its literal force — a word used only three times in the New Testament, here of an old woman’s crooked back made straight again. Ellicott explains why a bodily act was used at all: as with the blind and the dumb elsewhere, the touch was a help to the faith which had to be hers if she was to receive the full benefit of the power at work.

The praise that followed is read from its tense. Robertson marks the imperfect and calls it inchoative: she began glorifying God and kept it up. Ellicott says the same, that she poured out her joy in a continuous strain rather than a single exclamation. Barnes turns the detail into a rule, that those restored to health from sickness owe the restoring to God and should devote the life so given back to his service, as the fitting expression of their gratitude.

Calvin explains why the crowd’s reaction is recorded at all. It is mentioned so that we may know the cure was distinctly perceived to be a heavenly blessing: this was not some doubtful work which left room for argument on either side, but one that afforded ample and undoubted grounds for praising God. Calvin’s interest in the point is polemical rather than descriptive, since the unanimity of the bystanders is what throws the objection raised immediately afterwards into relief — a man finding fault with what everyone else in the building could see was a mercy.

Cyril finds a doctrinal point in the hands themselves. The word spoken he calls most suitable to God and full of heavenly majesty, since the disease is dispelled by a royal assent; but a hand is laid on her as well, and that is where he presses the answer to be given to certain objectors — the divine power had put on the sacred flesh, and the flesh was God’s own and no one else’s, not as though the Son of Man existed apart from the Son of God, which some have falsely thought. The same writer keeps the picture before him: a woman who had been creeping along the ground, raised upright by a single touch and telling out the mighty works of God.
14:
Gill begins with the office, insisting that a synagogue never had more than one ruler whatever some writers have said, and correcting a version which reads chief priests here, since those dwelt at Jerusalem. Robertson observes that nobody had addressed the man: he felt the weight of his position and was indignant, and though his anger was at Jesus he spoke to the crowd instead, using a word which really means must — a direct hit at one who had worked on the Sabbath. Robertson adds that the speech has a ludicrous sound, as though all anyone with a crooked back had to do was call round at his synagogue on a weekday; he had forgotten that this woman had been coming for eighteen years and gone away as she came.

Ellicott supplies the law being appealed to. Jewish tradition allowed a physician to practise his calling in an emergency, where life and death were at stake, but not in chronic complaints such as this one; and it is that restriction the ruler wished to impose as a check on the Healer in front of him. Barnes thinks the appeal self-defeating: had the man reasoned properly he would have seen that one able to perform such a miracle could not be a breaker of God’s law.

Calvin fastens on the indirection of the attack. The reprover does not venture to censure Christ openly, but turns the venom of his dislike on another quarter and condemns Christ in the person of the multitude, which Calvin calls an astonishing display of furious malice. He then presses the inconsistency of the ruling. If the six days are set apart for labour, why not forbid the people to enter the synagogue as well, lest they break the Sabbath by coming; why not order them to refrain from every exercise of godliness? And granting that men are kept from their own employments on that day, it is quite another thing to limit the grace of God by the same rule, and to bid sufferers come back on the other days for a cure, as if the power of God lay asleep on the Sabbath rather than being exerted on it chiefly, for the salvation of his people.

Barnes draws four inferences from the man’s behaviour. That people are often opposed to good being done because it is not being done in their own way and according to their own views. That they are readier to notice what they take for a breach of the law in others than the good those others may be doing. That the opposition falls not only on whoever does the good but on whoever is helped by it, this ruler seeming particularly annoyed that the people should come to be healed at all. And that such conduct is commonly the work of envy.
15:
Gill notes that the rebuke lands on the man who had not been addressed: the ruler had spoken to the people, but the thrust was at the healer, who knew it, and who answers in defence of what he had done and to expose the pretence behind the objection. Robertson calls the reply crushing and overwhelming, observes that the plural takes in the faultfinder and everyone agreeing with him, and notes the title used of Christ again in this narrative. Wesley says shortly that the motive of the complaint was envy and not the zeal for God’s glory it professed. Barnes reduces the argument to a sentence: you condemn me for doing to a woman what you do every week to a beast.

Basil defines the word from the theatre. A hypocrite is one who on the stage assumes a character not his own, and in life some men likewise carry one thing in the heart and show another on the surface. Chrysostom applies the definition: this man had the appearance of an observer of the law while his heart was crafty and envious, since what troubled him was not that the Sabbath was broken but that Christ was glorified. Chrysostom also compares the method used here with the method used elsewhere. Where a work is commanded, as when the paralytic was told to take up his bed, the words are raised to something higher and the hearers are convinced by the majesty of the Father; here, where everything is done by a word, nothing further is added at all, and the slander is answered out of the critics’ own practice. Cyril drives the reductio home: the law has not forbidden every kind of work, and if what is done by word and mouth were forbidden then men must stop eating and drinking and speaking and singing — and in any case, how is it manual labour to raise a woman upright by speaking to her?

Lightfoot shows from the rabbis how carefully the permission appealed to had been fenced. The disputation about how far a beast may be led out cautions that it must carry nothing which would count as a burden on that day, allowing a camel to be led with a halter and a horse with a collar when they go to pasture or to water; and the gloss adds that a horse may be taken to the water so that the collar may be dipped if the water is unclean. Robertson turns the same practice into the reproach it is meant to be, that these critics cared too much for an ox or an ass to leave it all the Sabbath without water, and notes in passing that the word for the stall is the word used of the manger at the Nativity.

Calvin finds a double comparison in the sentence and thinks one argument enough for so much malice and stupidity together. If it is lawful to perform the offices of humanity to cattle, it is ridiculous to suppose that the due observance of the day forbids assistance to the children of God. The two comparisons are of the cattle with the woman, and of the halter by which a beast is tied with the chains of Satan by which men are held bound to their destruction; so that the plea runs, you who are so scrupulous about the day venture to loose a beast, and why may not a like office of kindness be done to one of the elect people of God, where the necessity is a good deal more urgent?
16:
Robertson counts the argument in three steps, each one raising the claim: a human being and not an ox or an ass, a woman, a daughter of Abraham and so a Jewess — besides which she was old and ill. He marks the imperfect of necessity in the verb, that the healing simply had to be done, Sabbath or not. Wesley compresses it to two steps, any human creature being so far better than a beast, and much more this daughter of Abraham. Gill works the title hardest: she was not only a woman and a rational creature, preferable as such to an irrational one, but a descendant of the patriarch in whom the nation gloried, whose name was chosen for their women because it gave them a character above others — and besides this she was doubtless a good woman and a spiritual worshipper, a daughter of Abraham in the sense of walking in the steps of his faith. Barnes adds the edge: a ruler professing peculiar regard for the Jewish people as peculiarly favoured of God should have been the first to rejoice that she was loosed.

Cyril states the conviction bluntly. The ruler stands convicted of hypocrisy in that he leads his own cattle to water on the Sabbath, while this woman, who was no more a daughter of Abraham by birth than by faith, he thought unworthy to be loosed from the chain of her infirmity; he would rather she went on looking at the earth like the beasts than receive her natural stature, provided only that Christ was not magnified by it.

Who did the binding is taken as a statement of fact. Robertson says the words definitely assign the disease to Satan. Barnes explains the limits of that: it means Satan had inflicted the complaint, not that she was possessed, since possession commonly showed itself in derangement; God had suffered him to afflict her much as he was permitted to try Job, and it is no more improbable that God should allow Satan to inflict pain than that he should allow men to do it. Ellicott generalises the assumption, that the words imply a source beyond mere bodily disease, and at least in part the belief that very many forms of sickness are directly or indirectly traceable to the power of the Enemy, as Paul’s thorn in the flesh is called a messenger of Satan.

Ellicott ends with a guess about the writer. The narrative would have had a special interest for this Evangelist beyond what such stories had for the others, and we can scarcely help thinking of the beloved physician practising his own art for the good of men on the Sabbath as on other days — and being met, when he did, with words very like the ruler’s.
17:
Gill attributes the collapse of the opposition to the form of the argument: they had been reasoned with out of their own practice, and so strongly and rationally that the reasoning carried its own evidence and conviction. Cyril puts it more sharply, that they had nothing to answer because they had condemned themselves unanswerably. Robertson reads both halves of the verse from their tenses, an imperfect passive for the shaming — they went on blushing at the predicament they were in — and an imperfect active for the rejoicing, with the works that caused it in a present participle, continually being done. He calls the contrast between the emotions of the two groups a sharp one.

Cyril accounts for the difference between the two groups by what each brought with them. The people reaped great good from the miracles and rejoiced at the signs they saw, because the glory of the works vanquished every scruple in those who were not seeking him with corrupt hearts; where the adversaries, having come with the other disposition, found only the shame.

Barnes makes two sociological observations on it. The first is that those who opposed Christ were chiefly the rulers, who had an interest in doing so, since their popularity was at stake and they feared he would draw the people off from them. The second is that the common people heard him gladly and many of them believed, from which he concludes that the condition of the poor and of those in humble life is by far the most favourable for religion, and that most of the disciples of Jesus have been found there. The verse supports him at least in the division it reports, the adversaries named as a party and the people named as a whole.

On the closing phrase about glorious things Barnes supplies the Old Testament language it borrows, the song at the sea asking who is like the Lord, glorious in holiness, the psalm that calls his work honourable and glorious, and Isaiah’s promise of a branch that shall be beautiful and glorious. Gill keeps to the plainer sense, that what the people saw was the whole set of cures and sayings just recounted and not the one healing only, so that the rejoicing is a verdict on the day rather than on a single act.
18:
The Gloss supplies the join: while the adversaries stood ashamed and the people rejoiced at what had been done, the discourse turns to explaining the progress of the Gospel under a pair of similitudes. Robertson is less sure of the connection, since it is not clear what the inferential particle looks back to — the case of the woman, the enthusiasm of the crowd, or something this writer has not recorded. Henry explains why comparisons are used at all: the kingdom of the Messiah was still a mystery and people were generally in the dark and under mistakes about it, and when a thing is to be described to strangers it is described by likenesses — the burden of these two being that the kingdom will prove quite another thing from what the hearers expect. Gill notes only that the kingdom of God here is the kingdom of heaven of the other Gospels.

Ambrose connects the figure with its other use. Elsewhere a grain of mustard seed is brought in as the measure of faith; and if the mustard seed is the kingdom of God while faith is as the grain, then faith is truly that kingdom of heaven which is said to be within us. The grain itself is a mean and trifling thing, yet as soon as it is crushed it pours out its power, and faith too looks simple at first.

Bede reads the parable’s parts off one by one. The man is Christ and the garden his Church, to be cultivated by his discipline; and he is well said to have taken the grain, because the gifts he gave us with the Father out of his divinity he took from his humanity. The preaching grew and was spread through the whole world, and it grows in the mind of every believer too, since nobody is suddenly made perfect; but its growth is not that of grass, which soon withers, but of a tree rising up, whose branches are the manifold doctrines on which chaste souls, soaring upward on the wings of virtue, build and take their rest.

Theophylact gives the same allegory an inward turn. Any man who receives the word of the Gospel as a grain and sows it in the garden of his own soul makes it a great tree that puts out branches, and the birds of the air — meaning those who soar above the earth — settle in the branches, which is to say in sublime contemplation. He instances Paul, who received the instruction of Ananias as a small grain and, planting it in his garden, brought forth many good doctrines in which those with high heavenly thoughts have dwelt ever since. Barnes, Clarke and Wesley all decline to expound either parable here and send the reader to the fuller treatments in Matthew and Mark.
19:
Gill reads the comparison both ways at once, for the smallness at first and the increase afterwards, which is why the other two evangelists call it the least of all seed; and he applies all three senses of it — to the ministry of the Gospel, to the state of a Gospel church, and to the grace of God in the hearts of his people. Robertson identifies the plant as one of two species, both with small seeds and both growing to twelve feet on occasion, and records the Jewish proverb that made smallness and the mustard seed synonymous.

Robertson also notices that the ground is not the same ground as in the parallels. Where one has earth and the other a field, this has a garden — an old word standing only here and in the burial narrative of the fourth Gospel — and the phrase about becoming a tree he calls a common Hebraism, very frequent in the Greek Old Testament and in this writer alone among the evangelists.

Cyril of Jerusalem presses the seed’s disproportion between size and effect. The grain is small in bulk but fiery in operation, and though sown in a small space it throws out a circle of great branches and when grown can even shelter the fowls; so faith works the greatest effects in the soul in the swiftest moment. The soul enlightened by it has visions of God and beholds him so far as may be, ranges round the bounds of the universe, and before the end of this world already looks on the Judgment and on the payment of the promised rewards.

Ambrose takes the crushing of the seed as the point and runs it through three subjects. The martyrs are grains of mustard seed: they carry the sweet odour of faith about them, but hidden, until persecution comes and they are smitten by the sword, and so to the farthest boundaries of the world they scatter the seeds of their martyrdom. The Lord himself is a grain of mustard seed, who wished to be bruised that we might see ourselves to be a sweet savour of Christ, and who wished to be sown as such a grain, which a man takes and puts into his garden — for he was taken and buried in a garden, and rose again there, and became a tree. He is a grain while buried in the earth and a tree when lifted up into heaven, a tree overshadowing the world, in whose branches the fowls of the air rest: the heavenly powers, and those who for their spiritual deeds have been thought worthy to fly.
20:
Robertson notes that the question itself is peculiar to this Gospel, standing here and two verses earlier, while the parable it introduces is precisely the one given in Matthew. Gill records what is being added to what, the leaven hidden in three measures of meal following the grain of mustard seed, and remarks that the Syriac and Persic versions supply the subject which the Greek leaves understood. Wesley and Barnes again refer the exposition to the parallel place rather than repeat it here.

Ambrose reports a reading he does not quite adopt. Many think Christ himself is the leaven, since leaven made from meal excels its own kind in strength rather than in appearance; and so Christ, on the fathers’ account, shone out above others who were his equals in body but could not approach him in excellence. On that reading the woman of the parable stands as the type of the Holy Church.

His own preference turns the parts the other way about. We are the meal of the woman who hides the Lord Jesus in the secrets of our hearts, until the heat of heavenly wisdom penetrates our innermost recesses; and since the hiding was in three measures, Ambrose thinks it fitting to believe the Son of God hidden in the Law, veiled in the Prophets, and manifested in the preaching of the Gospel. Bede supplies the measure itself, a Palestinian unit holding about a bushel and a half, which makes the quantity of dough in the story a large one rather than a household baking.

Henry makes the repeated question the hinge of a second correction. The hearers expected the kingdom to make its way by external means, subduing nations and vanquishing armies, whereas it was to work like leaven, silently and insensibly and without force or violence; a little leaven leavens the whole lump, and so the doctrine of Christ would diffuse its relish through the world of mankind, the savour of the knowledge of it being made manifest in every place beyond anything one could have expected. The condition Henry attaches is time: the issue of the preaching has to be waited for, and whoever waits will find that it does wonders and alters the property of the souls of men.
21:
Gill describes the quality being compared: small in quantity but swelling and spreading, which fits the small beginnings of the Gospel ministry and its increase, the case of Gospel churches, and the nature of the grace of God. He then offers a darker alternative — that false doctrine may be meant instead, which got into the churches privately and by little and little and spread itself over them, as in the times of the papacy. Wesley fastens on the hiding, that for a time nothing of it appeared at all. Clarke and Barnes send the reader to the parallel for the rest.

Ambrose starts from what he takes to be the Lord’s own account of the figure, that the leaven is the spiritual teaching of the Church, and makes the three measures the man who receives it. The Church sanctifies with that leaven the man renewed in body, soul and spirit, these three being held in an equal measure of desire so that a complete harmony of will breathes out of them; and if in this life the three measures abide in one person until they are leavened and become one, there will be an incorruptible communion hereafter with those who love Christ. He offers a second distribution as well, the woman standing for the soul and the three measures for its three parts, the reasoning part, the affections and the desires, so that whoever hides the word of God in those three makes the whole spiritual, neither lying in argument by his reason nor being carried past control by anger or appetite.

Three further readings take the measures outside the individual. Augustine makes them the race of mankind, restored out of the three sons of Noah, and the woman who hid the leaven the wisdom of God. Eusebius makes the leaven the Holy Spirit, the Sower proceeding as it were from the seed which is the word of God, and the three measures the knowledge of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit which divine wisdom imparts. Bede makes the leaven love, which kindles and stirs up the heart, and the woman the Church, who hides that leaven in three measures because she bids us love God with the whole heart.
22:
Gill places the circuit in Galilee or Judea or both, the journey running from the one through the other to Jerusalem. Barnes narrows it to the towns lying between and reads diligence in the two participles: though on a journey the traveller remembered his work and did not excuse himself on the plea of haste, from which Barnes concludes that ministers should remember their Master neither concealed his character while travelling nor counted himself freed from the obligation to do good. Ellicott renders the phrase as making a journey, which implies a circuit deliberately planned, and takes it for the continuation of the one begun several chapters earlier, lying chiefly through the cities and villages of Peraea east of the Jordan — a stage implied in Matthew and Mark too, and in the retirement beyond Jordan recorded by John, which had led first through Samaria, then back to Samaria and Galilee, and so to Jericho. Robertson calls it the second of the journeys to Jerusalem in this later ministry, matching the one in the eleventh chapter of John, and notes the continuous tenses with the distributive preposition before cities and villages.

Calvin is not sure a single journey is in view at all. It may be that while he walked throughout Judea and visited each part of it to teach, he was accustomed to go up at the festivals; the first clause looks like a description of the course of life invariably pursued from the time the office committed to him was taken up, and to make the second agree the sense will be that when a feast drew near he attended the holy assemblies along with everyone else. Clarke takes the simpler line, that everything reported from the earlier chapter onwards is set down as done and said on the last journey to Jerusalem.

Theophylact draws a character out of the itinerary. He did not visit the small places only, as those do who wish to deceive the simple, nor the cities only, as those who are fond of display and seek their own glory, but went everywhere as the common Lord and Father who provides for all; nor did he keep to the country towns and avoid Jerusalem as though afraid of the lawyers’ cavils or of the death that might come of them, since where there were many sick, there the Physician chiefly showed himself. The Gloss ties the travelling back to the two parables: having spoken of how the teaching of the Gospel increases, he set about spreading it everywhere by preaching.
23:
Who asked, and in what spirit, is left open and variously guessed at. Gill says it was not one of the disciples but someone in the company, in one of the places along the road. Barnes also thinks him no disciple but one of the Jews, come either to perplex the teacher or to involve him in controversy with the Pharisees, and calls the question one of idle curiosity whose answer would have done little good, when it was far more important for the man to secure his own salvation than to indulge such speculations. Clarke is blunter still: a question of impertinence or curiosity, the answer to which can profit nobody, the grand question being whether the asker himself can be saved. Henry allows either a friend or a foe, noting that great liberty of questioning was given and that the answers went to the thoughts and intents of the heart; and he suspects a trap, since an answer that many would be saved would be reproached as loose and cheapening salvation, while an answer that few would be saved would be called precise and strait-laced.

Lightfoot explains why the motive is hard to read: the received opinion among the Jews was that all Israel should have a part in the world to come, so that the question may have been captious or may have been sincere. He shows the matter disputed among the rabbis themselves, one teacher applying the enlarged mouth of hell to the man who forsakes a single statute, another refusing to have Israel judged so and holding that a man who has learned but one statute shall escape. Barnes reports the comparison used on the stricter side, that as only two of all the hosts who came out of Egypt entered Canaan, so a proportionally small number would enter heaven. Robertson sums it up as an academic theological problem with the rabbis, the number of the elect.

Ellicott insists on the tense of the participle, which is present and not perfect: those who are being saved, or who are in the way of salvation. He leaves open whether the questioner meant salvation in the higher sense or safety from the destruction lately threatened, thinks the two may well have been blended in his mind, and holds that the answer points clearly to the first. Calvin suggests what prompted the question. One who declared himself the author of life could gather only a small number of disciples, so that it might look as though a little band were to be saved and the whole church going to ruin, since the nation adopted by God as the heir of life had rejected his teaching almost to a man; and Calvin admits that a similar doubt steals over us whenever we look at the melancholy condition of the world.

The Gloss refers the question back to the parable just told, where the birds of the air rested in the branches, from which a hearer might suppose that many would obtain the rest of salvation; and it notes that since one man had asked for everybody, the answer is not given to him individually. Gregory makes the evasion deliberate and defends it. It was the Saviour’s custom to answer those who put useless questions not according to what they judged proper but with regard to what might profit the hearers; and what advantage would it have been to those standing there to know whether the saved would be many or few, when it was far more necessary to know the way by which a man comes to salvation? So nothing is said to the idle question, and the discourse is turned to a weightier subject.
24:
The verb is what every one of them stops on. Barnes takes it literally as to agonize, a word out of the Grecian games, where men in races and wrestlings put forth all their powers for the victory before thousands of spectators, trained long for the conflict, the honour of winning being among the highest a people could give; so the command is to be diligent, active and earnest, and to make the overcoming of sinful propensities the first business of a life. Robertson notes that the middle plural takes in others besides the questioner, and that the kindred noun is used of the struggle in Gethsemane. Wesley reduces it to a phrase, strive as in an agony, adding that barely seeking will not avail. Ellicott marks the variation from the parallel, struggle as the wrestler struggles in place of the simple command to enter, with the whole illustration compressed, and calls it another case of general teaching adapted to a particular occasion. Gill spells out the content of the striving: diligence in the use of means, searching the Scriptures with care, constant attendance on the preaching of the word, earnest prayer for light and grace, contending with every enemy that opposes the soul’s salvation, and bearing reproach and persecution through to the prize of an incorruptible crown.

Robertson adds a small architectural observation that changes the picture. In Matthew the narrow gate is an outside gate, in the wall; the word here is the entrance to a house, so that what is being pressed through is a narrow door, and the crowd outside is on a doorstep rather than on a road.

Calvin explains why the second half of the verse is attached to the first. It was added so that we might not be deceived by a vain hope, as if the multitude of our companions would be of any use to us. The flesh is willing to flatter itself, and many who give themselves every indulgence promise themselves an easy entrance into life; so men practise a mutual deception on one another and fall asleep in wicked indifference. To shake those flattering hopes off his own people, Christ declares that the very men who reckon their possession of life already certain will be the ones shut out. Clarke makes the same distinction shortly: they seek, that is they wish and desire, but they do not strive, and not being in earnest they do not get in.

The fathers take the narrowness as a description of the Christian life rather than of the number saved. Basil contrasts the two breadths: departure from the right is exceedingly broad, so that whoever leaves the path to the kingdom finds himself in a vast extent of error, while the right way is narrow and the slightest turning aside is dangerous, as on a bridge, where whoever slips to either side goes into the river. Cyril makes the gate stand for the toils and sufferings of the saints, since as a victory in battle testifies to the strength of the soldiers, so a courageous endurance of labours and temptations makes a man strong. Chrysostom then has to reconcile this with the easy yoke and light burden promised elsewhere, and does so by distinguishing the two points of view: the one was said of the nature of temptations and the other of the feeling of those who overcame them, since whatever is troublesome to our nature may be counted easy once it is undertaken heartily — and besides, it is narrow only at the entrance and opens into a large space, where the broad one runs the other way. Gregory notices which word comes first, that striving is named before the gate because unless the mind struggles manfully the wave of the world is not overcome, by which the soul is thrown back again into the deep.
25:
Barnes explains the figure from ordinary housekeeping. A householder willing to see his friends keeps his doors open at the proper time, but there is also a proper time for closing them, and at night it would be improper and vain to seek entrance, the house being shut; so there is a proper time to seek entrance into heaven and there will be a time when it is too late. Gill reads the rising up as rising from table, the entertainment being over — the Gospel feast at an end, all the effectually called guests come in, and long forbearance already used towards the rest — and identifies the master of the house as the bridegroom of the church, the head of the body, the King of saints, Son over his own house and high priest there.

Bede makes the within and the without a matter of degrees of presence. Christ, being very God, is everywhere, and is said to be already within those whom, though he is in heaven, he gladdens with his visible presence, while he is as it were outside those whom he helps secretly as they contend on this pilgrimage. He will enter in when he brings the whole Church to the contemplation of himself, and will shut the door when he takes from the reprobate all room for repentance; and those who then stand outside and knock will be the men who, cut off from the righteous, implore in vain the mercy they had despised.

Robertson finds the construction awkward and the division of the passage disputed: it may run on from the previous verse without a break, though Bruce argues for two parables, the earlier about being in earnest and this one about being too late — and Robertson thinks both points are certainly here. He marks the effective aorist with its perfective preposition, the door not merely closed but slammed fast. Clarke and Ellicott send the reader to Matthew, Ellicott observing that the passage holds elements common at once to two separate places there.

Calvin presses what the shut door costs the men outside. Having declared that the door will not open to many who wish to enter, the discourse now asserts that they gain nothing by occupying a place in the church, since God will at length arise in judgment and shut out of his kingdom those who presently lay claim to a place in his family; and Calvin works the comparison of a householder who, having learned that some dissolute members of his own establishment slip out unnoticed at night and leave the house open to thieves, refuses to let the night-prowlers back in. Wesley adds the sting that even agonising will not avail once the door is shut, so the agonising must be done now, by faith, prayer, holiness and patience; and of their standing outside he remarks that till then they had not thought of it, asking how new that sense of their misery will be, how late, and how lasting.
26:
Gill notes that the words are spoken in the speakers’ own favour and with a view to being let in. Barnes explains why they should count for anything: to have eaten with a man is evidence of acquaintance or friendship, so the plea is that the pleader was a professed follower and had some ground for thinking himself a friend. There is no allusion to the sacrament here, the figure being taken from the ordinary customs of men; and the second clause is offered as further proof — you favoured us as though you loved us, you did not turn away from us and we did not drive you off.

Ellicott prefers the plain past tense, that we ate and drank and thou didst teach, and marks the difference from the parallel, where higher claims are put into the speakers’ mouths and they ask whether they did not prophesy in his name. There the speakers stand for men holding office in the Church of God who have never truly submitted to the divine Teacher; here the words point to actual companionship, and to hopes built on having once sat at meat in the house of a publican or a Pharisee with the Prophet they acknowledged as the Christ — though in its wider application the plea covers everyone who in any sense eats and drinks with him now in the visible fellowship of his Church.

Cyril and Theophylact fix the first reference on Israel. Cyril recalls the practice of their law, where those offering victims to God eat and are merry, and the reading of the books of Moses in the synagogues, who delivered in his writings not his own words but God’s. Theophylact makes the claim simpler still, that Christ was born of them according to the flesh, so that they ate and drank with him and heard him preach; and he turns it on his own readers, since we eat the body of Christ and drink his blood as often as we approach the mystic table, and he teaches in the streets of our souls so far as those are open to receive him. Bede allegorises the two verbs: whoever eagerly receives the food of the word eats and drinks in the Lord’s presence, Scripture in its obscurer places being food, since by being expounded it is as it were broken and swallowed, and in its clearer places drink, taken down just as it is found. But the banquet does not delight the guest whom the piety of faith fails to commend.

Robertson calls it grotesque to claim credit because Christ had taught in their streets, and allows only that the speakers are hard run for excuses. Calvin makes the same point doctrinally: it will be of no advantage to the Jews that he came near them and allowed them familiar intercourse with him, if when called they do not answer at the appointed day. He notes too that the figure is dropped at this point, since the speaker now states without any comparison that he is himself the judge, words which can apply to nobody else.
27:
Robertson says the blunt statement cuts the matter short and sweeps away the flimsy cobwebs, since acquaintance with Christ in the flesh does not open the door. He traces the quotation to the psalm, as in Matthew, but with a different phrase for the workers of iniquity and a different imperative for the departing. Gill records the addition made by the Persic version, bidding them be gone from his sight and far from his door, and reads in it indignation and abhorrence, as of one who cannot bear them near him. Barnes and Wesley refer the exposition to the parallel place.

Gregory explains what the disclaimer means, since omniscience cannot be in question. For God not to know is for him to reject, in the way that a man who speaks the truth is said not to know how to lie: not that he would be at a loss if he wished to lie, but that from love of truth he scorns to say what is false. So the light of truth does not know the darkness which it condemns, and the sentence is a refusal rather than a confession of ignorance.

Bede draws the conclusion that bears on the pleas just made: knowledge of the Scriptures does not make a man known to God when the iniquity of his works proves him unworthy. Augustine, reading the same exchange, finds the questioner’s premise conceded rather than refuted — there really are few who enter by the strait gate, as another saying has it that narrow is the way which leads to life and few there are who find it — which is why the warning about many seeking and failing comes in immediately afterwards. Bede supplies the motive and the obstacle together: they are urged on by love of their own safety, and stopped by fright at the roughness of the road.

Basil describes the choice the description looks back on. The soul wavers to and fro, choosing virtue at one moment when it considers eternity and preferring pleasures at the next when it looks to the present; on one side it sees ease and the delights of the flesh, on the other subjection and a captive’s bondage; here drunkenness and there sobriety, here wanton mirth and there a flood of tears, here dancing and there praying, here the sound of the pipe and there weeping, here lust and there chastity. The sentence pronounced at the door names the men who settled that wavering the wrong way, and names them by their works rather than by their professions.
28:
Robertson fixes the scene from one adverb: the word means out there, outside the house from which they have been driven, and the participle describing their expulsion is present passive and continuous — they are being cast out, with the door already shut. Gill places the weeping and gnashing at the moment the sentence and the character are heard, and says it will be increased by what follows. Robertson also records a textual wrinkle in the verb of seeing, where the editors put a future in the margin against the aorist subjunctive of the text, unless one is willing to allow here the kind of future subjunctive that later Greek developed under Latin influence. Barnes, Clarke and Wesley all refer the figures to the parallel in Matthew, where they are explained at length.

Bede finds two distinct punishments named rather than one described twice. The feeling of cold and of heat are both in view, since weeping is commonly excited by heat and the gnashing of teeth by cold; or else, on his second suggestion, the gnashing betrays the feeling of indignation, the man who repents too late being also too late in growing angry with himself. The Gloss matches each to the sin it answers: the teeth will gnash which here delighted in eating, the eyes will weep which here wandered with desire, and by both of them the real resurrection of the wicked is represented rather than a figure of it.

Theophylact names the particular sting for the particular hearers. The words are addressed to Israelites, and their severest blow is just this, that the Gentiles have rest with the fathers while they themselves are shut out. Calvin presses the descent they were relying on. They bore no resemblance to the holy fathers and had no right to boast of being sprung from them, yet nothing was commoner than the abuse of the title of the Church, which they always had in their mouths; and a bastard race which has departed from the faith and piety of the fathers has no inheritance. Calvin hears a silent reproof in it besides: men who wanted companions in seeking salvation never thought of associating themselves with the fathers, but looked round among their contemporaries, who had degenerated from that example into innumerable corruptions.
29:
Gill reads the coming as universal in extent and pointed in application: from all parts of the world and every nation under heaven, meaning the Gentiles, which will aggravate the punishment of the Jews and cause still more rage. Clarke says the same more flatly, that the Gentiles in every part of the world would receive the Gospel of the grace of God once the Jews had rejected it. Robertson notes that the future passive means to recline, the figure being that of a heavenly banquet, and enters a caution: the saying does not mean that these will be saved in different ways, only that many will come from all four quarters of the earth.

Calvin reads the verse as calculated provocation. The larger illustration is drawn from the fact that the Jews, who reckoned themselves the only lawful heirs of God, were to be rejected and the Gentiles put in their place, obtaining the life promised to Abraham and his posterity; and the contrast is set up to excite them to faith by a holy jealousy, as Paul writes that he will count it a distinguished honour of his ministry if he can stir any of his own nation and blood to such emulation. They must have been stung by it, Calvin adds, having an inordinate love of themselves and proudly despising God and his gifts.

Eusebius explains why these three names are the ones used. The fathers mentioned lived before the times of the Law, and forsaking the sins of many gods to follow the Gospel way they received the knowledge of the most high God; many of the Gentiles were conformed to them by a similar manner of life, while their own children suffered estrangement from the Gospel rules. Augustine takes the occasion to reconcile the few of the earlier verse with the many of this one: they are few in comparison with those who are lost and many when united with the angels, and they scarcely seem a grain while the threshing floor is being swept, yet so great a mass will come off that floor as will fill the granary.
30:
Ellicott dates the saying as well as explaining it. In point of time this is the first utterance of the great law that God’s judgment reverses man’s, so that when the words are used later of the young ruler they are a fresh application of a law already laid down. Here the application is primarily national: Israel had been the first of nations and was to become, in its outward fortunes, the last, while the heathen who had been without hope and without God in the world would gain the pre-eminence of being heirs of the kingdom — the individual application growing naturally out of the national one. Robertson adds only that the saying was repeated many times afterwards.

Calvin keeps the sentence narrowly polemical. All that was intended here, he says, was to throw down the vain confidence of men who, having been chosen by God in preference to all the rest of the world, trusted to that distinction and imagined God in a manner bound to them; so their condition is threatened with a swift change, the Gentiles who were then cast off taking the first rank and the Jews, stripped of their honour, not holding even the lowest place or some small corner in the Church. Wesley states the double reckoning: many of the Gentiles latest called shall be most highly rewarded, and many of the Jews first called shall have no reward at all. Gill makes the exchange concrete, the Gentiles who were mean and abject, far from God and aliens from the commonwealth of Israel and called last of all, sitting down among patriarchs and prophets in the kingdom of heaven and enjoying the same glory with them. Cyril puts the whole thing in a line, that the Gentiles have been preferred to the Jews who held the first place.

Theophylact turns the law round on his own readers before they can enjoy it. We, it seems, are the first, having taken in the rudiments of Christian teaching from our very cradles, and we may well prove last in comparison with heathens who believed at the end of their lives. Bede sets out four reversals in a row: many at first burning with zeal afterwards grow cold; many at first cold become warm all at once; many despised in this world will be glorified in the world to come; and others renowned among men will be condemned in the end.
31:
Robertson notes the hour as this writer’s favourite way of marking time, and then the oddity of the scene: here the Pharisees appear in a new role, warning Jesus against the machinations of Herod while they are plotting themselves. Gill explains how they came to be there, since there were Pharisees in every part of the country, and what had nettled them — the parables delivered that day, the miracles, and the striking things said which they knew applied to themselves. On his reading the warning is their stratagem rather than the Tetrarch’s, though he allows that Herod may have used these men to frighten a prisoner he dared not take, held back partly by the people and partly by the terror still on his own mind for what he had done to John.

Ellicott sets out the three possibilities and chooses one. This is the only intimation anywhere of such a purpose, so the question is whether the Pharisees reported what they knew out of feelings more or less friendly, invented a tale to be rid of his presence, or were sent by Herod to deliver a threat; and the answer returned, with its message to the fox, points to the last as the likeliest. He grants that Herod is elsewhere said to have desired for a long season to see him, but holds that oscillations between vague curiosity and vague fear suited the man’s character. Barnes thinks the story probable enough on its face, since Herod had killed John, knew that Jesus was drawing the people away, and might be expected to fear one who so resembled the man he had killed; yet he allows it more than possible that Herod sent the messengers, Jesus being too popular for an open execution and the Tetrarch wanting him gone. Henry reports the view that the Pharisees had no ground at all and framed the story to drive him out of Galilee, where his interest was great and growing, and into Judea, where men really did seek his life — though he notices that the reply is addressed to Herod himself, which suggests they had something to go on. Wesley allows in a line that the caution may have been given out of good will.

Cyril supplies a motive of a different kind.
