The words just spoken had roused the Pharisees to anger, because they could see the people smitten in their hearts and eagerly receiving his faith; and for fear of losing their office as rulers of the people, and their gains with it, they urge him to leave under a pretended concern for him — which is why one who searches the heart and the reins answers meekly and under a figure. Clarke fixes the jurisdiction at Galilee or Peraea, beyond which Herod had no authority, and cites Lactantius for the claim that this Herod was the chief instigator of the Jewish rulers against Christ, afraid of being driven from his own kingdom if another were allowed to set one up.
32:
Barnes defines the epithet before applying it: a fox is the emblem of slyness, cunning and artful mischief, and the word serves also for a dissembler; what is alluded to is not the man’s vices but his artifice, the attempt to clear him out of the territory by a stratagem. Robertson reads cowardice into it as well as cunning, in a man who had put the Baptist to death and wanted this preacher in his power despite his superstitious fears, and takes the message to mean independence of the plots of Herod and Pharisees alike — adding that preachers are often put in a tight place by politicians quite willing to see them shorn of real power. Ellicott notices that the Greek word is always feminine, which lends a touch of indignant force: the Tetrarch had so identified himself with Herodias that he had lost his manliness, and the proverbial type of the worst form of a woman’s craft fitted him. Wesley calls the name proper for subtlety and cowardice together.

Clarke raises a difficulty about the fit. Herod was a vicious prince living in open incest, and a character implying cunning and the concealment of evil intentions sits oddly on a man who never seemed studious to conceal anything — unless the speaker, knowing his heart, saw him covering a desire for Christ’s destruction under a pretence of zeal for the law and the people’s welfare. Clarke adds that among the Jews the fox was the emblem of a wicked ruler who combined cunning with cruelty and was forever plotting to enrich himself by spoiling the people. Gill keeps the other candidate open, that the word may be aimed at the Pharisees and their craft in framing the story, professing good will while meaning only to scare him out of their country; and he notes the Jewish use of the word for a vain and empty man as against a good one. Calvin is sure the person meant is Herod Antipas, but thinks the term aimed less at the cunning of his whole life than at the insidious methods by which he worked to undermine the doctrine of the Gospel where he did not venture to attack it openly.

On what the reply actually says, Barnes paraphrases it as an announcement rather than a defiance: tell him that I am working miracles in his territory and shall go on doing so, being neither afraid of his art nor of his enmity but engaged in my proper work. Ellicott thinks the message answers a wish Herod is known to have had, since he hoped to see some miracle done, and is told that the time for such sights was all but over. Lightfoot finds a proverb behind the reply — worship the fox in his time, which the gloss explains as the time of his prosperity — and reads the answer as a refusal to do any such thing, however the man may wallow in his present fortune. Calvin and Robertson both take the last clause as pointing past Herod altogether, Calvin having Christ acknowledge that he will discharge the office enjoined on him and then be offered in sacrifice at the end of his course, and Robertson noting the present passive of a verb that means being brought to completion.

Augustine reads the three days as the history of the Church rather than a timetable. The words are spoken mystically of his body: devils are cast out when the Gentiles forsake their superstition and believe, and the cures are perfected when, after the renouncing of the devil and of this world and at the end of the resurrection — by which the third day is as it were completed — the Church is perfected in angelical fullness by the immortality of the body also.
33:
Ellicott prefers a stronger verb, that he must journey or go onward, the word being the one used earlier of the face set towards Jerusalem, and takes it to carry the same intensity of conviction and purpose. Gill notes that the Syriac and Arabic read it as I must work, in the sense of going about doing good, casting out devils and healing diseases. Clarke reports Kypke’s contention that the right rendering is that he must walk today and tomorrow in the neighbouring coasts, which would make the clause a statement of itinerary rather than of destiny.

The three days divide the commentators again. Theophylact explains the phrase as idiom: today and tomorrow signify many days, as we say in conversation that today and tomorrow such a thing happens without meaning it falls within that interval; and he would repunctuate the sentence, putting a stop after today and tomorrow and then adding the walking on the day following, since in reckoning one says the Lord’s day and the day after, and on the third I will go out, counting two in order to name the third. Ellicott refuses the literal sense outright, since there were not three days to pass before the entry into Jerusalem and it would not have been true in fact; the formula conveys a short undefined interval, and he thinks this would be obvious were men better able to enter into the poetic forms of Eastern speech. Robertson simply calls it a proverb. Barnes reads it as a little time and fills in the sense: I must remain here this short while and do cures, and then depart, not for fear of Herod but because my time will have come.

The clause about Jerusalem is taken as irony with an edge. Robertson calls it a severely ironical indictment of the city, and observes that the shadow of the Cross reaches as far as the Peraea where the speaker now stands. Wesley says the city claims prescription for murdering the messengers of God, such cruelty and malice not being found elsewhere. Calvin turns the sentence on the men who brought the warning: the danger they hold out is an idle bugbear, and he has Christ ask whether it is they, whom he foresees will be his executioners, that advise him to beware of somebody else. The reproof runs much farther, since the city might be said to have been for a long period a den of robbers in which almost all the prophets had been murdered.

Lightfoot supplies the machinery that made the saying literally true. A tribe, a false prophet or a high priest could be judged only by the bench of seventy-one; and such a man was not tried to death in the court of his own city, nor at Jabneh, but brought up to the great Consistory at Jerusalem and reserved for one of the feasts, when the execution was carried out so that all Israel should hear and fear and do no more so. On that rule the city was the only lawful place for the death of a prophet, which is what the clause says, and what the men who had come to frighten him out of Galilee had evidently not considered.
34:
Whether the lament was uttered twice is argued on both sides. Gill notices that in Matthew the words are delivered in the temple at Jerusalem while here they are spoken in Galilee, inside Herod’s jurisdiction, so that the same words appear to have been used at different times, in different places and to different hearers — unless this writer took them from Matthew and inserted them here because the perishing of a prophet at Jerusalem had just been mentioned. Robertson weighs the same question: the connection suits either place, Plummer calls it a rather violent hypothesis to suppose the words spoken twice, and it is possible, though unlike this writer’s usual method, that the mention of the city drew them in; but Robertson can see no real difficulty in the lament being made in both. He notes that the two Gospels use different infinitives of the same double compound, and that the question how often carries its own evidence, showing repeated visits to Jerusalem which are otherwise known only from John. Wesley counts three solemn visits made since the baptism for this very purpose.

Bede fixes what is being addressed: not the stones and buildings of the city but the people living in it, wept over with the affection of a father. Chrysostom makes the doubling of the name the whole tone of the sentence, a token of compassion or of very great love, the Lord speaking, if it may be said so, as a lover would speak to a mistress who had despised him and was on that account about to be punished. A Greek expositor adds the other half of the effect, that the repetition also makes the rebuke severe: she who knew God is the one now persecuting God’s ministers.

Cyril proves their unmindfulness of the divine blessings out of the clause itself, since the gathering had been attempted again and again: he led them by the hand of Moses out of all wisdom, he warned them by his prophets, and he wished to gather them still. Clarke notes that the metaphor of the hen can be illustrated from the Greek Anthology. Cyril of Jerusalem turns the same words against a crude picture of God: some imagined him a man with wings, from a true text ill understood about hiding under the shadow of his wings, forgetting that the Only-begotten speaks in the same way of gathering children as a hen gathers her chickens — so that what was meant for God’s protecting power was taken for a body, and men who failed to understand the figure sank to the level of things human.

Barnes draws out what the message to Herod teaches, now that the lament has shown where the danger really lay. That our lives are safe in the hands of God, and that wicked men can do no more to injure us than he permits. That we should go on fearlessly in doing our duty, and especially if we are doing good, without regarding the threats of men. And that we should be on our guard against crafty and unprincipled men, who often profess to seek our good while they are plotting our ruin — even those who come professedly from our enemies to caution us being frequently enemies themselves.
35:
Clarke makes everything turn on the pronoun. It is the temple, called here your house and not mine: I acknowledge it no longer, I have abandoned it and will dwell in it no more. He compares the phrase used when the temple was given over to the Chaldeans, the house of your sanctuary, and the Lord’s word to Moses about thy people, which intimated that he no longer acknowledged them for his followers. Clarke adds that some understand not the temple but the whole commonwealth of the Jews. Gill says only that city and temple alike would be desolate in a little time. Theophylact reads it as a tenancy ended: so long as there was virtue in them it was his temple, and after that it was theirs.

Basil and Bede both take the image from birds. Basil compares the sons of Jerusalem to birds in the net: those used to flying in the air are caught by the treacherous devices of the catchers, but you shall be as a chicken wanting another’s protection, and when your mother has flown away you are taken from the nest, too weak to defend yourself and too feeble to fly. Bede carries the figure into history: the city which had been called a nest is now called the house of the Jews, for when the Lord was slain the Romans came and plundered it like a deserted nest, taking away their place, their nation and their kingdom together.

Lightfoot confesses that the last clause defeats him, and says so with unusual candour: there was a time when he saw no difficulty in the words at all, and now, which may seem a paradox, his old eyes see better than his younger ones did, for the more he looks into the passage the more obscure it appears. In what sense can it be said that they shall not see him, when after this, at least as the words stand in this evangelist, they saw him among them for three months and more — and in a singular manner in that august triumph when, riding upon an ass, he received the acclamations of the people in these very words? One might therefore think the sentence had respect to that very occasion, but the placing of it in Matthew tells against the thought.

Wesley takes the clause the other way and does not look for a sight of Christ in it at all. The house is now irrecoverably consigned to desolation, and after a very short space they shall not see him until the time comes when, taught by their calamities, they are ready and disposed to say that blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. On that reading the words do not imply that they should see Jesus then, but only that they would earnestly wish for the Messiah and in their extremity be ready to entertain anyone who assumed the character. Barnes supplies the Old Testament language of desolation standing behind the first half — the sanctuaries made waste in Leviticus, the habitation left desolate in the psalm, the land made a wilderness in Isaiah — and refers the rest to the parallel in Matthew.
